intro.why: Attention removed the fixed-length bottleneck of seq2seq models and became the core operation of the Transformer (Module 9), and therefore of BERT, GPT and modern LLMs, vision Transformers and multimodal models.

symbols: number of heads (or hidden size in additive attention)

sections.title: Why study encoder–decoder models?
sections.plain: Input and output lengths differ.
sections.body: Many NLP tasks require variable-length sequence-to-sequence mapping: sentiment analysis ("The phone battery lasts only 2 hours. Very disappointed." → "Negative"); question answering (context + "What is the capital of India?" → "New Delhi"); text summarisation (500-word article → 50-word summary). Key observation: input length $T\ne$ output length $T'$ in general.

sections.title: The challenge: standard RNN limitations
sections.plain: An RNN emits one output per input step.
sections.body: A standard RNN produces one output per input step, requiring $T=T'$ (figure: $x_1..x_4\to h_1..h_4\to y_1..y_4$). Example: "India gained independence from Britain. What year was independence?" (10 words) should give "1947" (1 word), but a standard RNN produces 10 outputs. Solution needed: separate the reading phase from the generation phase.

sections.title: Encoder–decoder architecture
sections.plain: Encoder compresses input into c; decoder generates from c.
sections.body: Two-stage process: (1) encoder reads and compresses the entire input into a context vector $\mathbf c$; (2) decoder generates the output sequence from the context, one token at a time. Figure: "What is capital" → encoder → $\mathbf c$ (fixed size) → decoder → "New Delhi". Flexibility: input length $T$ can differ from output length $T'$.

sections.title: How encoder–decoder works; QA example
sections.plain: c = h_T^enc; decoder starts from c and feeds back its outputs.
sections.body:
Phase 1, encoding:

$$h_t^{enc}=\phi(W_{hh}^{enc}h_{t-1}^{enc}+W_{hx}^{enc}x_t+b_h^{enc}),\qquad \mathbf c=h_T^{enc}$$

Phase 2, decoding: initialise $h_0^{dec}=\mathbf c$ and generate autoregressively:

$$h_t^{dec}=\phi(W_{hh}^{dec}h_{t-1}^{dec}+W_{hy}^{dec}y_{t-1}+b_h^{dec}),\qquad P(y_t\mid y_{QA example: context "India gained independence in 1947. Gandhi led the movement.", question "What year was independence?", answer "1947". The encoder reads the entire input ($T\approx15$ tokens); $\mathbf c$ encodes "answer is about year and independence"; the decoder generates "1947" then ⟨END⟩ ($T'=1$ meaningful token).

sections.title: Training vs inference; exposure bias
sections.plain: Teacher forcing in training, own predictions at inference.
sections.body: Training (teacher forcing): feed the ground-truth $y_{t-1}$ as decoder input at each step. Inference (free running): start from $y_0$ = ⟨START⟩ and feed back the model's own predictions $\hat y_{t-1}$. Exposure bias: the decoder is trained on ground truth but tested on its own (possibly wrong) predictions, so early mistakes can compound. Mitigations: scheduled sampling, beam search, sequence-level training.

sections.title: The critical problem: the context bottleneck
sections.plain: Everything squeezed into one fixed vector; early tokens get lost.
sections.body:
All input information must pass through the fixed-size vector $\mathbf c$. Problems: (1) information loss: long sequences → early tokens forgotten; (2) fixed capacity: e.g. 512 dimensions limit storage; (3) uniform encoding: all input parts weighted equally, no selectivity. Example: a 50-word review compressed to 512 numbers, then used to generate the sentiment.

Concrete example: a 30-word laptop review ("…Initial impressions were good. Fast delivery. However, after 2 weeks, battery drains in 2 hours. Screen flickers constantly. Very disappointed. Would not recommend.") compressed into a 512-dim $\mathbf c$: early positive sentiment may be lost or key phrases weakened; when generating "Negative" the decoder needs to emphasise the later parts, but $\mathbf c$ treats all parts equally.

Why fixed context fails: information about early tokens in $\mathbf c$ decays with input position until later tokens dominate. Observations (Sutskever et al., 2014): performance degrades for sequences beyond ≈30 tokens; the first words are often lost by generation time; long-range dependencies are hard. (Sutskever et al. mitigated this partly by reversing the source sentence.)

sections.title: The solution: attention
sections.plain: A different context c_t at every decoder step.
sections.body: Core insight: instead of a single fixed context, let the decoder selectively attend to relevant input parts at each step. Figure: encoder states $h_1..h_5$ with weights $\alpha=(0.05,0.50,0.30,0.10,0.05)$ feeding a dynamic $\mathbf c_t$ for decoder state $s_t$. Differences: before, one context for the whole decoding; after, a different $\mathbf c_t$ at each step $t$; weights $\alpha_i$ learned automatically from data; focus on relevant positions dynamically.

sections.title: Attention: definition
sections.plain: A weighted sum of values, weights from query–key similarity.
sections.body:
Definition: attention computes a weighted sum of values based on the similarity between a query and keys. Components: query $\mathbf q$ (what we're looking for: decoder state), keys $\{\mathbf k_i\}$ (what's available to match: encoder states), values $\{\mathbf v_i\}$ (content to retrieve: encoder states).

$$\text{Attention}(\mathbf q,\{\mathbf k_i,\mathbf v_i\}_{i=1}^n)=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\mathbf v_i,\qquad \alpha_i=\frac{\exp(\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i))}{\sum_{j=1}^n\exp(\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_j))}$$

Because the weights are a softmax, the output is a convex combination of the values: it lies in their convex hull, and attention is differentiable end to end.

sections.title: Core concept: weighted combinations
sections.plain: Not all inputs contribute equally.
sections.body: Key principle: not all inputs contribute equally; attention learns relevance. Without attention: output $=f(\sum_{i=1}^nx_i)$ (uniform weighting); with attention: output $=f(\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_ix_i)$ (learned weights $\alpha_i$). Constraint: $\sum_i\alpha_i=1$ (a probability distribution).

sections.title: Worked examples: gold prices, sentiment, Q&A
sections.plain: Recent days, 'excellent', and 'Delhi' get the largest weights.
sections.body:
Example 1: gold price. Predict tomorrow's price (₹/gram) from the past 7 days [6200, 6180, 6150, 6250, 6280, 6270, 6300]. Recent days (5–7) receive higher weights:

$$\mathbf c\approx0.03(6200)+0.05(6180)+0.07(6150)+0.15(6250)+0.25(6280)+0.23(6270)+0.22(6300)\approx6261$$

(verified: 6261.1; these weights sum to 1). The accompanying figure shows different weights (0, 0, 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.22) that sum to only 0.72.

Example 2: sentiment. "The product quality is excellent but delivery was very slow": weights The 0.02, product 0.15, quality 0.2, is 0.02, excellent 0.35, but 0.08, delivery 0.1, slow 0.08 (sum 1.00). The model learns "excellent" ($\alpha_5=0.35$) is most important for sentiment despite the negative "slow" → Positive. (The word list omits "was very"; weights still sum to 1.)

Example 3: Q&A. Context "Mumbai is the financial capital. Delhi is the national capital."; question "What is the national capital?". Weights Mumbai 0.05, is 0.02, financial 0.08, capital 0.03, Delhi 0.45, is 0.02, national 0.2, capital 0.15 → answer "Delhi". Highest attention on "Delhi" ($\alpha_5=0.45$), secondary on "national" (0.20) and "capital" (0.15); the model correctly ignores "financial capital".

sections.title: Without vs with attention
sections.plain: Fixed c vs dynamic c_t.
sections.body:
Without attentionWith attention
ContextOne fixed bottleneck $\mathbf c$Dynamic $\mathbf c_t$ per step
InformationLoss for long inputsSelective focus
Long sequencesPoorHandled well

Key difference: the context adapts to what the decoder needs at each step. Bonus: the weights $\alpha_{t,i}$ are inspectable (soft alignments), although attention weights are not a guaranteed explanation of a model's decision.

sections.title: Attention as information retrieval
sections.plain: Like a soft database lookup.
sections.body: Analogy: attention works like a database lookup. A memory (key–value store): Mumbai → Info1, Delhi → Info2, Bangalore → Info3. The query "What is the national capital?" goes through similarity matching against the keys, softmax gives weights, and the retrieved weighted context mostly comes from Info2. Process: (1) the query searches memory via key similarity; (2) attention weights from query–key match; (3) retrieve values weighted by attention. Unlike a hard lookup (exact match, one result), attention returns a differentiable blend of all values.

sections.title: Query–key–value components and mechanics
sections.plain: Score, softmax, weighted sum.
sections.body:
Three roles: query $\mathbf q$: what information are we seeking? From the decoder state ("I need to generate the next word"), e.g. the state when generating "Delhi". Keys $\{\mathbf k_i\}$: what's available to match against? From encoder states (representations of input tokens [Mumbai, is, financial, capital, Delhi, …]). Values $\{\mathbf v_i\}$: what content do we retrieve? Also from encoder states (often the same as keys). Intuition: the query searches keys and retrieves matching values.

Step by step:

$$e_i=\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)\ (i=1..n),\qquad \alpha_i=\frac{\exp(e_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n\exp(e_j)}\ \Big(\textstyle\sum_i\alpha_i=1\Big),\qquad \mathbf c=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\mathbf v_i$$

Visual: $\mathbf q$ compared with $\mathbf k_1..\mathbf k_4$ gives $\alpha=(0.1,0.5,0.3,0.1)$, applied to $\mathbf v_1..\mathbf v_4$ to form $\mathbf c$. Separating keys from values lets the "address" used for matching differ from the content returned.

sections.title: Attention as weighted pooling
sections.plain: Max = hard pick, average = uniform, attention = learned weights.
sections.body: Pooling perspective: attention is soft, adaptive pooling over a sequence. For values (3, 7, 2, 5): max pooling = 7 (hard selection); average pooling = 4.25 (uniform weights); attention pooling $\sum\alpha_iv_i$ with learned weights (0.1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2) = 0.3 + 3.5 + 0.4 + 1.0 = 5.2. Key difference: max/average are fixed, uniform aggregations; attention is data-dependent, learned aggregation based on the query. As the softmax temperature → 0 attention approaches max-like hard selection; as it → ∞, averaging.

sections.title: Dot-product attention
sections.plain: score = qᵀk.
sections.body:
$$\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)=\mathbf q^T\mathbf k_i=\sum_{j=1}^dq_jk_{i,j},\qquad \alpha_i=\frac{\exp(\mathbf q^T\mathbf k_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^n\exp(\mathbf q^T\mathbf k_j)}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf q^TK^T)_i$$

with $K=[\mathbf k_1,\dots,\mathbf k_n]^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$. The simplest form: similarity via inner product (large when vectors point the same way and are long). No parameters; requires $d_q=d_k$.

sections.title: Example: dot-product attention
sections.body: Stock example: $\mathbf q=[0.8,0.6]^T$ (tomorrow's expected trend features); keys $\mathbf k_1=[0.5,0.3]^T$, $\mathbf k_2=[0.9,0.7]^T$, $\mathbf k_3=[0.4,0.2]^T$. Scores $e_1=0.8(0.5)+0.6(0.3)=0.58$, $e_2=0.72+0.42=1.14$ (highest), $e_3=0.32+0.12=0.44$. Softmax: $e^{0.58}=1.786$, $e^{1.14}=3.127$, $e^{0.44}=1.553$, sum 6.466, so $\alpha=(0.276,0.484,0.240)$ (code ex1). A commonly quoted version prints $(0.21,0.62,0.17)$, which is not the softmax of these scores (it sums to 1.00 but corresponds to scores roughly twice as spread). The interpretation holds: day 2 is most aligned with the query and gets the most attention.

sections.title: Scaled dot-product attention and why scaling matters
sections.plain: Divide by √d_k so softmax doesn't saturate.
sections.body:
Problem: for large $d$, dot products grow large and softmax saturates. Solution (Vaswani et al., 2017): scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$:

$$\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k)=\frac{\mathbf q^T\mathbf k}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad \text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$

Derivation. If the components of $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf k$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then $\mathbb E[\mathbf q^T\mathbf k]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(\mathbf q^T\mathbf k)=\sum_{j=1}^{d_k}\mathrm{Var}(q_jk_j)=d_k$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance regardless of dimension (code ex1: variance 4.2, 62.8, 501 for $d=4,64,512$).

Benefits: scores stay in a reasonable range; prevents vanishing softmax gradients; standard in all Transformers. Gradient flow: without scaling ($d=512$) scores spread over ±20 and the softmax is pushed to 0/1 where $\partial\alpha/\partial e\approx0$ (saturated); with scaling, scores sit in the sensitive region with healthy gradients, which is critical for training deep (6–24+ layer) networks.

sections.title: Additive (Bahdanau) attention
sections.plain: score = vᵀ tanh(W_q q + W_k k): a tiny MLP.
sections.body:
$$\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i)=\mathbf v^T\tanh(W_q\mathbf q+W_k\mathbf k_i)$$

with $W_q\in\mathbb R^{h\times d_q}$ (query projection), $W_k\in\mathbb R^{h\times d_k}$ (key projection), $\mathbf v\in\mathbb R^h$ (learnable vector), $h$ hidden dimension (hyperparameter, e.g. 256). Flow: $\mathbf q\to W_q$, $\mathbf k_i\to W_k$, add, tanh, $\mathbf v^T$ → $e_i$. Advantage: handles $d_q\ne d_k$. It is the original attention mechanism for neural machine translation. Efficiency trick: $W_k\mathbf k_i$ can be precomputed once per source sentence.

sections.title: Comparing scoring functions and their cost
sections.plain: Dot-product: fast matrix multiply; additive: more flexible, slower.
sections.body:
Aspect Dot-product (scaled)Additive (Bahdanau)
Formula$\mathbf q^T\mathbf k/\sqrt{d_k}$$\mathbf v^T\tanh(W_q\mathbf q+W_k\mathbf k)$
ParametersNone$W_q,W_k,\mathbf v$
Complexity per pair$O(d)$$O(d\cdot h+h)$
ExpressivenessBilinear/linear similarityNon-linear (tanh)
ParallelisationExcellent (matrix multiply)Moderate
DimensionsRequires $d_q=d_k$Works with $d_q\ne d_k$
Modern usageTransformersEarly seq2seq

Historical note: additive was better for RNN models (2014–2016) but scaled dot-product dominates in the Transformer era (2017+). Complexity for sequence length $n$, dimension $d$ and $m$ queries: scores $O(mnd)$ vs $O(mndh+mnh)$; softmax $O(mn)$ both; weighted sum $O(mnd)$ both; totals $O(mnd)$ vs $O(mndh)$. Batch form: $QK^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ in one GPU operation; highly parallel; memory $O(mn)$ for the attention matrix. In practice dot-product is 3–5× faster thanks to hardware utilisation.

Method ScoreParameters
Dot product$\mathbf q^T\mathbf k$None
Scaled dot product$\mathbf q^T\mathbf k/\sqrt{d_k}$None
Additive (Bahdanau)$\mathbf v^T\tanh(W_q\mathbf q+W_k\mathbf k)$$W_q,W_k,\mathbf v$
Multiplicative (Luong)$\mathbf q^TW\mathbf k$$W$

Trade-offs: dot product fast but requires $d_q=d_k$; scaled prevents saturation (Transformer default); additive more expressive, flexible dimensions, more parameters. Multiplicative handles $d_q\ne d_k$ with $W\in\mathbb R^{d_q\times d_k}$.

sections.title: Bahdanau attention: the breakthrough
sections.plain: c_t = Σ α_{t,i} h_i, with α from s_{t−1} and h_i.
sections.body:
Key innovation (Bahdanau et al., 2014): replace the fixed context with dynamic attention. Encoder states $h_1..h_5$ with weights $\alpha_{t,1..5}$ → attention → $\mathbf c_t$ → decoder $s_t$ → $y_t$. $\mathbf c_t=\sum_{i=1}^T\alpha_{t,i}h_i$ where $\alpha_{t,i}$ depends on the previous decoder state $s_{t-1}$ and encoder state $h_i$.

At each decoder step $t$:

$$e_{t,i}=\mathbf v^T\tanh(W_ss_{t-1}+W_hh_i)\quad(\text{1. alignment scores})$$$$\alpha_{t,i}=\frac{\exp(e_{t,i})}{\sum_{j=1}^T\exp(e_{t,j})}\quad(\text{2. weights}),\qquad \mathbf c_t=\sum_{i=1}^T\alpha_{t,i}h_i\quad(\text{3. context})$$$$s_t=\text{RNN}([y_{t-1};\mathbf c_t],s_{t-1})\quad(\text{4. decoder state}),\qquad P(y_t\mid y_{(Luong attention instead scores with the current state $s_t$ and combines afterwards.)

sections.title: Bidirectional encoder
sections.plain: h_i = [forward; backward] sees both sides.
sections.body:
$$\overrightarrow h_i=\text{RNN}_{fwd}(x_i,\overrightarrow h_{i-1}),\qquad \overleftarrow h_i=\text{RNN}_{bwd}(x_i,\overleftarrow h_{i+1}),\qquad h_i=[\overrightarrow h_i;\overleftarrow h_i]$$

Bahdanau used a bidirectional RNN encoder to capture context from both directions; benefit: $h_i$ encodes both past and future context for position $i$, so each annotation describes its word in context.

sections.title: Attention alignment and a Q&A example
sections.plain: Translation weights form a near-diagonal alignment.
sections.body:
Hindi → English: "yah kitaab bahut achchhi hai" → "This book is very good". The attention matrix shows a strong (near-)diagonal pattern: word-level alignment, e.g. "yah" ↔ "This" (α = 0.85), "kitaab" ↔ "book" (α = 0.82); the heatmap also aligns "is" ↔ "hai", "very" ↔ "bahut", "good" ↔ "achchhi", showing reordering (Hindi puts the verb last). Another common illustration has "book" attending to "kitaab" with α ≈ 0.85 and "good" → "achchhi" 0.78; the numbers are illustrative.

Q&A: context "Mumbai is the financial capital. The Reserve Bank is located there.", question "Where is Reserve Bank?", answer "Mumbai". The decoder focuses on context mentioning "Reserve Bank" and "Mumbai", with the highest weight (α = 0.55) on "Mumbai": it extracts the answer from the relevant part of the input.

sections.title: Attention types: taxonomy
sections.plain: Self, cross, masked, multi-head.
sections.body:
TypeQ sourceK, V sourceUse case
Self-attentionSame sequenceSame sequenceIntra-sequence relationships
Cross-attentionSequence ASequence BInter-sequence alignment (seq2seq)
Masked attentionSame sequenceSame (causal mask)Autoregressive generation
Multi-headSame (parallel)Same (parallel)Multiple relationship types

Key distinctions: source of Q, K, V; masking (what can attend to what); purpose (which relationships are modelled).

sections.title: Self-attention: definition and purpose
sections.plain: Q, K, V all from the same sequence.
sections.body:
$$Q=XW_Q,\qquad K=XW_K,\qquad V=XW_V,\qquad X=[\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n]^T$$

Purpose: model relationships within a sequence. Time series: gold prices over 24 hours [₹6,180, ₹6,200, …, ₹6,280]: each hour attends to all others, e.g. hour 24 attends strongly to hours 17, 10, 3 (7-hour periodicity), capturing temporal patterns automatically. Text: "The student didn't pass the exam because he was unprepared": self-attention helps "he" attend to "student", resolving coreference and capturing long-range dependencies.

sections.title: Cross-attention: inter-sequence alignment
sections.plain: Queries from one sequence, keys/values from another.
sections.body:
$$Q=X_AW_Q,\qquad K=X_BW_K,\qquad V=X_BW_V$$

Time series: multivariate forecasting where sequence A (stock prices, the current state) queries sequence B (economic indicators: inflation, GDP, interest rates), e.g. gold price queries inflation and USD exchange rate. Text: Hindi → English, with sequence A the English words being generated (decoder) and B the Hindi source (encoder); when generating "book" the decoder attends to "kitaab". Visualisation: "This" → "yah" (0.85), "book" → "kitaab" (0.82), "good" → "achchhi" (0.78). This is exactly Bahdanau attention: the original cross-attention mechanism.

sections.title: Masked (causal) attention
sections.plain: Add −∞ to future positions before softmax.
sections.body:
$$\text{Mask}_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&j\le i\ \text{(allowed)}\\-\infty&j>i\ \text{(masked)}\end{cases},\qquad \text{Attention}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+\text{Mask}\right)V$$

Self-attention with a causal constraint: a position can only attend to the past. Time series: predicting the price at time $t$ using only $1..t-1$; the mask prevents attending to $t+1,t+2,\dots$, so no "cheating" during training (predict tomorrow's gold price without seeing tomorrow's actual price). Text: GPT-style language modelling, "The customer was very ___": the token at position 5 ("very") can only attend to positions 1–4; future tokens are invisible during training and inference; generation is autoregressive, left to right. (Strictly, with $j\le i$ allowed, "very" also attends to itself.)

Visualisation: for "The customer was very happy with service" the allowed cells form a lower-triangular pattern: token $i$ only sees tokens $\le i$. Implementation: add $-\infty$ to masked positions before softmax → weight 0. This lets a whole sequence be trained in parallel while each position behaves causally.

sections.title: Multi-head attention
sections.plain: Several attention heads in parallel, concatenated and projected.
sections.body:
Motivation: a single attention may miss different types of relationships; use multiple heads in parallel, each learning different patterns. Time series with 3 heads: short-term trends (last 2–3 days), weekly patterns (7-day cycles), monthly patterns (30-day trends); combined: a richer representation. Text with 3 heads: a syntax head (subject–verb–object: "The customer complained", the verb attends to the subject); a semantic head (meaning and coreference: "he" → "customer"); a positional head (adjacent dependencies: "very happy").

$$\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W_O,\qquad \text{head}_i=\text{Attention}(QW_i^Q,KW_i^K,VW_i^V)$$

Typical hyperparameters: $h=8$ heads, $d_{model}=512$, $d_k=d_v=64$ per head. Splitting $d_{model}$ across heads keeps the cost roughly that of one full-width head; parameters per layer $4d_{model}^2$ (1,048,576 for 512, ignoring biases).

sections.title: When to use which attention type
sections.plain: Self for context, cross for two sequences, masked for generation, multi-head everywhere.
sections.body:
TypeUse when
Self-attentionModelling relationships within a sequence; contextual representations (BERT encoder); long-range dependencies in text or time series
Cross-attentionAligning two sequences (seq2seq): translation, summarisation, question answering; Transformer decoder attending to encoder outputs
MaskedAutoregressive generation (language modelling); preventing leakage from the future; GPT-style models, time-series forecasting
Multi-headCapturing diverse relationship types simultaneously; all modern Transformers (BERT, GPT, T5, ViT)

sections.title: Self-attention: formal definition
sections.plain: Z = softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V: every output mixes all inputs.
sections.body:
Given $X=[\mathbf x_1,\dots,\mathbf x_n]\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}$: (1) linear projections $Q=XW_Q$, $K=XW_K$, $V=XW_V$; (2) scaled dot-product attention $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^T/\sqrt{d_k})V$; (3) output $Z=\text{Attention}(Q,K,V)\in\mathbb R^{n\times d_v}$. Key property: every output $\mathbf z_i$ is a weighted combination of all inputs $\{\mathbf x_j\}_{j=1}^n$. Difference from RNNs: direct connections between all positions, no sequential bottleneck.

SelfAttention(X):                       # X: n × d
  Q, K, V = X·W_Q, X·W_K, X·W_V          # O(n d²)
  S = Q·Kᵀ / √d_k  (+ mask)              # n × n, O(n² d)
  A = softmax(S, row-wise)               # rows sum to 1
  return A·V                             # O(n² d)

sections.title: The position-invariance problem
sections.plain: Shuffling tokens just shuffles outputs: order is invisible.
sections.body:
Critical issue: self-attention is permutation-invariant: "The customer was happy with service" and "service with happy was customer The" are treated identically, because attention weights depend only on content, not position. Word order matters in NLP ("Dog bites man" ≠ "Man bites dog"), so we need position information: inject it into the input embeddings.

Precisely, self-attention is permutation equivariant: $\text{Attention}(PX)=P\,\text{Attention}(X)$ for any permutation matrix $P$ (each token's output is unchanged, just reordered), verified numerically in code ex2. The $\text{Attention}(X)=\text{Attention}(PX)$ holds only for a pooled (order-free) summary of the outputs.

sections.title: Positional encoding: learned and sinusoidal
sections.plain: x̃_i = x_i + p_i; sinusoids of geometrically spaced frequencies.
sections.body:
Add position information to input embeddings: $\tilde{\mathbf x}_i=\mathbf x_i+\mathbf p_i$. Two approaches: (1) learned positional embeddings (BERT, GPT-2): $\mathbf p_i$ is a learned parameter per position; simple but doesn't generalise beyond the training length. (2) Fixed sinusoidal encoding (original Transformer): $\mathbf p_i$ computed with sine/cosine; deterministic; generalises to any length.

$$PE(pos,2i)=\sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right),\qquad PE(pos,2i+1)=\cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right)$$

pos: position $0,1,2,\dots$; $i$: dimension index $0..d_{model}/2-1$; $d_{model}$: model dimension (e.g. 512). Intuition: different dimensions use different frequencies; lower dimensions have higher frequency (fine-grained position), higher dimensions lower frequency (long-range); each position gets a unique encoding vector. (A commonly quoted version says "lower dimensions = lower frequency"; with $\omega_i=1/10000^{2i/d}$ it is the other way round: $i=0$ has wavelength $2\pi$, the last pair ≈$2\pi\cdot10000$.) Modern alternatives: relative position biases, RoPE (rotary embeddings, which apply exactly the rotation below to queries and keys), ALiBi.

sections.title: Why sinusoidal encoding works
sections.plain: PE(pos + k) is a fixed linear (rotation) map of PE(pos).
sections.body:
Key property: for any fixed offset $k$, $PE(pos+k)$ is a linear function of $PE(pos)$: $PE(pos+k,2i)=M_k\cdot PE(pos,2i)$ for some matrix $M_k$. With $\omega_i=1/10000^{2i/d}$ and the identities $\sin(\alpha+\beta)=\sin\alpha\cos\beta+\cos\alpha\sin\beta$, $\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta$:

$$\begin{bmatrix}PE(pos+k,2i)\\PE(pos+k,2i+1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos k\omega_i&\sin k\omega_i\\-\sin k\omega_i&\cos k\omega_i\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}PE(pos,2i)\\PE(pos,2i+1)\end{bmatrix}$$

i.e. $\sin((pos+k)\omega_i)=\sin(pos\,\omega_i)\cos(k\omega_i)+\cos(pos\,\omega_i)\sin(k\omega_i)$: a linear combination of $PE(pos,2i)$ and $PE(pos,2i+1)$, with $M_k$ independent of $pos$ (a block-diagonal rotation; verified in code ex2). Benefit: the model can learn to attend by relative position ("3 positions back"). Also $PE(p)\cdot PE(p+k)=\sum_i\cos(k\omega_i)$ depends only on $k$.

sections.title: Summary and key formulas
sections.plain: Attention = soft lookup; scaled dot-product; types; positional encoding.
sections.body:
Summary: (1) attention: dynamic weighted aggregation based on relevance; QKV framework for information retrieval; solves the bottleneck by attending selectively. (2) Scoring: dot-product (simple, fast); scaled dot-product (prevents saturation, Transformer default); additive (more expressive, slower). (3) Types: self (intra-sequence), cross (inter-sequence), masked (causal), multi-head (diverse patterns). (4) Positional encoding: required for position-aware self-attention; sinusoidal is fixed and generalisable.

Key formulas:

$$\text{Attention}(\mathbf q,\{\mathbf k_i,\mathbf v_i\})=\sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\mathbf v_i,\ \alpha_i=\mathrm{softmax}(\text{score}(\mathbf q,\mathbf k_i));\qquad \text{Attention}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V$$$$\text{MultiHead}(Q,K,V)=\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1,\dots,\text{head}_h)W_O;\qquad PE(pos,2i)=\sin\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}},\ PE(pos,2i+1)=\cos\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}$$

sections.title: Further comparisons and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "Attention weights explain the model." They show where information was mixed from, not necessarily why a decision was made; different weight patterns can give the same output.
  • "Self-attention understands word order." Not without positional information; it is permutation-equivariant.
  • "Scaling by √d_k is just a tuning trick." It follows from the variance of a sum of $d_k$ products.
  • "Masking is only for inference." It's essential in training too, to stop the model peeking at the targets it must predict.
  • "Multi-head attention multiplies the cost by h." Heads use $d_k=d_{model}/h$, so total cost is about that of one full-width head.

code.title: Attention scores and weights: the session's examples
code.explain: Recomputes the gold-price context (6261), attention pooling (5.2), the dot-product example (correct weights 0.276, 0.484, 0.240), the variance argument for √d_k scaling, additive scores, a causal mask and the cost comparison.
mistakes: Forgetting to subtract the max before exp (overflow).
Normalising over the wrong axis (columns instead of rows).
code.code:
# Attention as weighted averaging: the session's examples recomputed (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
softmax = lambda e: np.exp(e - e.max()) / np.exp(e - e.max()).sum()
# Gold-price example: weights from the formula line
prices = np.array([6200, 6180, 6150, 6250, 6280, 6270, 6300.])
a = np.array([0.03, 0.05, 0.07, 0.15, 0.25, 0.23, 0.22]); print("weights sum", a.sum(), " context c =", round(a @ prices, 1))
fig = np.array([0, 0, 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.2, 0.22]); print("figure's weights sum to", fig.sum(), "(not a distribution)")
# Attention pooling vs max/avg 
v = np.array([3, 7, 2, 5.]); w = np.array([0.1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.2]); print("max", v.max(), " avg", v.mean(), " attention", w @ v)
# Dot-product attention example 
q = np.array([0.8, 0.6]); K = np.array([[0.5, 0.3], [0.9, 0.7], [0.4, 0.2]])
e = K @ q; print("scores", e, " softmax", softmax(e), " (reference values: 0.21, 0.62, 0.17)")
print("scaled by sqrt(2):", softmax(e / np.sqrt(2)))
# Why scale: dot products of random d-dim vectors have variance d
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for d in (4, 64, 512):
    Q = rng.normal(size=(2000, d)); Kk = rng.normal(size=(2000, d)); s = (Q * Kk).sum(1)
    P = np.array([softmax(rng.normal(size=10) * np.sqrt(d)) for _ in range(500)])
    Ps = np.array([softmax(rng.normal(size=10)) for _ in range(500)])
    print(f"d={d:3d}: var(q.k)={s.var():7.1f}  mean max-weight unscaled {P.max(1).mean():.2f}, scaled {Ps.max(1).mean():.2f}")
# Additive (Bahdanau) attention with small illustrative weights
Wq = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (3, 2)); Wk = rng.normal(0, 0.5, (3, 2)); vv = rng.normal(0, 0.5, 3)
e_add = np.array([vv @ np.tanh(Wq @ q + Wk @ k) for k in K]); print("additive scores", e_add, " weights", softmax(e_add))
# Causal mask 
n = 4; S = rng.normal(size=(n, n)); M = np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), 1)
A = np.exp(S + M - (S + M).max(1, keepdims=True)); A /= A.sum(1, keepdims=True); print("causal attention weights:\n", A)
# Complexity comparison: multiply counts
n, d, h = 512, 64, 256
print(f"scaled dot-product scores n*n*d = {n*n*d:,};  additive n*n*(d*h + h) approx {n*n*(d*h + h):,}")

code.title: Self-attention, multi-head attention and positional encoding
code.explain: Self-attention from scratch, a check that Attention(PX) = P·Attention(X), a two-head layer, a causal mask, sinusoidal encodings and a numerical check that PE(pos + k) = PE(pos)·M_k for a fixed rotation M_k.
mistakes: Adding positional encodings after attention instead of to the inputs.
Using −1e4 instead of −∞ in half precision (can still leak probability).
code.notes: nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=512, num_heads=8, batch_first=True); learned positions: nn.Embedding(max_len, d_model).
code.code:
# Self-attention, multi-head attention and sinusoidal positional encoding from scratch (NumPy)
import numpy as np
np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
def softmax(Z, axis=-1): Z = Z - Z.max(axis, keepdims=True); E = np.exp(Z); return E / E.sum(axis, keepdims=True)
def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(K.shape[1])
    if mask is not None: S = np.where(mask, S, -np.inf)
    A = softmax(S); return A @ V, A
n, d = 5, 8
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); WQ, WK, WV = (rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (d, d)) for _ in range(3))
Z, A = attention(X @ WQ, X @ WK, X @ WV); print("attention weights (rows sum to 1):\n", A, "\nrow sums", A.sum(1))
# permutation: shuffling the tokens just shuffles the outputs (equivariance), so order is invisible
P = np.eye(n)[[4, 2, 0, 1, 3]]; Zp, _ = attention(P @ X @ WQ, P @ X @ WK, P @ X @ WV)
print("Attention(PX) == P Attention(X):", np.allclose(Zp, P @ Z))
# multi-head: h heads of size d/h, concatenated and projected
h = 2; dk = d // h; heads = []
for i in range(h):
    Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (d, dk)) for _ in range(3)); heads.append(attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)[0])
WO = rng.normal(0, d ** -0.5, (d, d)); MH = np.concatenate(heads, 1) @ WO; print("multi-head output shape", MH.shape)
print("parameters per MHA layer with d_model=512 (4 d^2, no biases):", 4 * 512 * 512)
# causal mask
causal = np.tril(np.ones((n, n), bool)); _, Ac = attention(X @ WQ, X @ WK, X @ WV, causal); print("causal weights upper triangle all zero:", np.allclose(np.triu(Ac, 1), 0))
# sinusoidal positional encoding
def pe(pos, dm):
    i = np.arange(dm // 2); w = 1 / 10000 ** (2 * i / dm); P = np.zeros((len(pos), dm))
    P[:, 0::2] = np.sin(np.outer(pos, w)); P[:, 1::2] = np.cos(np.outer(pos, w)); return P
E = pe(np.arange(50), 16); print("PE(pos=1)[:6] =", E[1, :6])
# PE(pos + k) is a fixed linear map (rotation) of PE(pos), for every pos
k = 3; dm = 16; w = 1 / 10000 ** (2 * np.arange(dm // 2) / dm); M = np.zeros((dm, dm))
for j, om in enumerate(w): c, s = np.cos(k * om), np.sin(k * om); M[2*j:2*j+2, 2*j:2*j+2] = [[c, -s], [s, c]]
print("PE(pos+3) == PE(pos) @ M for all pos:", np.allclose(E[3:], E[:-3] @ M))
print("dot products PE(10).PE(10+k) for k=0..5:", np.round([E[10] @ E[10 + kk] for kk in range(6)], 2))
